method: symmetric four-world authoring, post-hoc seeded key selection

items.setting: Airport baggage service office: a baggage agent at the counter speaks with a passenger whose checked suitcase did not appear on the carousel.

worlds.keyAct: asks to collect it on the spot
worlds.line: We found your suitcase — it arrived on the later Chicago flight.
worlds.reply: Could I pick it up at this counter right now?
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The agent says the suitcase has been found and has already arrived, so asking to collect it at the counter right away is the natural next step. Wondering whether it stays in Chicago until tomorrow contradicts the announced arrival, and describing a red ribbon is pointless once the bag is identified. There is also no claim form in play, so a phone number has nothing to be added to.

kills.1: Since the agent says "it arrived on the later Chicago flight", asking whether it stays there until tomorrow's first flight contradicts the stated arrival.
kills.2: "We found your suitcase" means the bag is already identified, so volunteering a ribbon description to help locate it is pointless.
kills.3: The agent says "found your suitcase" and requests no paperwork, so "on here" has no form to refer to.

worlds.keyAct: checks how long it stays put
worlds.line: I'm sorry, but your suitcase is still sitting in Chicago.
worlds.reply: So it stays there until the first flight tomorrow?
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: Told the suitcase is still sitting in Chicago, the passenger naturally checks how long it will stay there before the next flight brings it over. Asking to pick it up at this counter right now is impossible for a bag in another city, and a ribbon description was never requested. Offering a phone number presupposes a claim form that was never mentioned.

kills.0: With the bag "still sitting in Chicago", there is nothing at this counter to pick up right now.
kills.2: The agent already tracks the bag — "your suitcase is still" located — so no identifying ribbon description was asked for.
kills.3: "I'm sorry, but" opens a report of bad news, not paperwork, so there is no form for a phone number to go on.

worlds.line: Does your suitcase have any tags or stickers on the outside?
worlds.reply: It has a red ribbon tied around the handle.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The agent asks what marks the suitcase carries, and naming the red ribbon around the handle answers exactly that. Asking to pick the bag up now ignores that it has not yet been located, and musing that it stays somewhere until tomorrow invents a delay nobody reported. A phone number belongs on a form, and no form has been offered.

kills.0: A question about "any tags or stickers" means the bag has not been located, so it cannot be picked up at the counter now.
kills.1: Asking about "tags or stickers on the outside" reports no delay or location, so there is no "there" for the bag to stay in.
kills.3: "Does your suitcase have" opens a question, not a claim form, so a phone number has nowhere to go.

worlds.keyAct: asks a clarifying question about the form
worlds.line: Please fill out this claim form with your local address.
worlds.reply: Do you also need my phone number on here?
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: Handed a claim form that wants a local address, the passenger sensibly checks whether a phone number should go on it too. Asking to pick the bag up now clashes with the fact that a claim is being filed at all, and inferring that it stays somewhere until tomorrow has no stated basis. The ribbon description answers a question about appearance that was never asked.

kills.0: Being told to "fill out this claim form" means the bag is missing, so it cannot be collected at the counter right now.
kills.1: The request for "your local address" states no location or delay, so asking whether it stays there has no referent.
kills.2: The form wants "your local address", and nobody asked what the bag looks like, so the ribbon description answers nothing.

items.setting: Hotel front desk: a receptionist and a departing guest discuss a late checkout on the morning of departure.

worlds.line: Which room are you in, and under whose name?
worlds.reply: Room five twelve, booked under the name Park.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk asks for the room and the name, and reciting both answers the question directly. Protesting about a conference pushes against a deadline nobody has imposed, and calling a midnight window plenty refers to a storage offer never made. Doubting the printed noon time presupposes a correction that has not been issued.

kills.1: The clerk only asks "under whose name" the room is booked and imposes no deadline, so there is no ruling for a conference conflict to protest.
kills.2: "Which room are you in" mentions no luggage window, so calling midnight plenty refers to nothing.
kills.3: Asking which "room are you in" issues no correction, so no printed noon time has been called into doubt.

worlds.line: I'm afraid noon is firm — the room turns over today.
worlds.reply: But my conference here doesn't finish until three o'clock.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: Told that noon cannot move, the guest pushes back with the real conflict: the conference runs until three. Reciting a room number and name answers a question that was not asked, and praising a midnight storage window responds to an offer never made. Calling the printed noon time wrong contradicts a clerk who has just confirmed noon.

kills.0: The clerk states "noon is firm" rather than asking anything, so reciting a room and name answers no question.
kills.2: Because "the room turns over" at noon and no midnight storage was offered, nothing here is plenty of time.
kills.3: Since "noon is firm", the printed noon time is confirmed, not wrong.

worlds.line: If it helps, we can store your luggage until midnight.
worlds.reply: Until midnight is plenty — my train leaves at ten.
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: Offered luggage storage until midnight, the guest confirms the window comfortably covers a ten o'clock train. Reciting a room and name answers no question here, and the conference objection has nothing to push against since storage until midnight outlasts an event ending at three. Doubting a printed noon time responds to a correction nobody made.

kills.0: An offer to "store your luggage" asks for no room or name, so reciting them answers nothing.
kills.1: Storage running "until midnight" easily outlasts a conference ending at three, so there is no conflict to protest.
kills.3: "If it helps" extends a favor and states no checkout rule, so no printed time has been contradicted.

worlds.line: Actually, your booking already includes checkout at four o'clock.
worlds.reply: Then the noon time printed on my key sleeve is wrong?
worlds.explanationIfSpoken: The clerk corrects the record — checkout is already four — so the guest reasonably checks whether the noon time printed on the key sleeve is simply wrong. Reciting a room and name answers no question, and the conference objection is moot when four o'clock already covers an event ending at three. Praising a midnight window responds to a storage offer that was never made.

kills.0: "Your booking already" includes late checkout is an assertion, not a question, so reciting a room and name hangs.
kills.1: With "checkout at four o'clock" included, a conference ending at three fits comfortably, leaving nothing to protest.
kills.2: The line grants "checkout at four" and offers no luggage storage, so calling a midnight window plenty has no referent.
